unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5 of your Year 8 English course. In this unit, you will explore the important topic of natural resources and sustainability. You will learn how communities around the world—and especially in East Africa—depend on natural resources like water, fish, forests, and clean air, and what happens when those resources are threatened by pollution, carelessness, or outdated practices.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: Natural Resources Under Pressure
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every community on Earth depends on natural resources, though we rarely notice them until they begin to disappear. Natural resources are the materials and systems that nature provides free of charge: fresh water, fertile soil, fish, forests, minerals, and clean air. Along the coastlines of East Africa, these resources are woven into daily life. Families drink and cook with water drawn from wells and rivers. Fishing crews supply the markets with the day's catch. Mangrove forests shelter young fish, protect villages from storms, and provide timber for boats and homes. When these systems are healthy, they quietly support everything else: food, work, trade, and even the air we breathe.
The problem is that healthy appearances can be deceptive. A stretch of sea may look pristine from the beach, blue and calm and inviting, while beneath the surface the coral is dying and the fish stocks are collapsing. Scientists describe this as the gap between how an ecosystem looks and how it actually functions. By the time the damage becomes visible to everyone, it has often grown severe. That is why so many environmental problems seem to arrive suddenly, when in truth they have been building slowly for years.
Three pressures do most of the damage. The first is pollution: plastic bags, bottles, chemical waste and engine oil wash into rivers and drift out to sea, where they poison fish and choke coral. The second is overuse. In many coastal towns, the transition from small family fishing boats to large commercial trawlers has multiplied the size of the catch. When the amount taken from the sea begins to surpass what the sea can replace, populations of fish shrink year after year. The third pressure is habit. Communities repeat old practices, such as burning rubbish on the beach or dumping waste behind the market, simply because they have always done so, without asking whether conditions have changed.
Forests face the same arithmetic. Across East Africa, trees are cut for charcoal, timber and farmland faster than seedlings can replace them. When a hillside loses its trees, the soil washes into the rivers with every storm, the rivers carry the mud down to the coast, and fishing grounds slowly choke. Clean air, the quietest resource of all, suffers wherever rubbish is burned in the open. Each resource is connected to the others, which is why damage in one place so often appears as an unwelcome surprise somewhere else.
Sustainability is the idea that answers these pressures. A practice is sustainable when it meets the needs of people today without destroying the resources that people will need tomorrow. Sustainability does not demand that communities abandon fishing or farming. Instead, it asks them to modify how they work: to take less, to waste less, and to give damaged ecosystems time to recover so that the harm can subside naturally. A fishing crew that respects breeding seasons, a market that provides bins, and a school that teaches children to test water quality are all practising sustainability.
Who is responsible for protecting natural resources? The honest answer is everyone, but young people have a special part to play. They will live longest with the consequences of today's choices, and they are often the quickest to learn new methods. Around the world, student groups now monitor rivers, replant forests and campaign for cleaner streets, producing copious evidence that ordinary citizens can change what governments and industries overlook. The obstacles they face are rarely villains; more often they are ordinary habits defended by people who mean no harm.
A polluted coastline is not the end of the story. Given protection and time, seas can recover, forests can regrow, and dismal grey rivers can run clear again. But recovery only begins when a community faces the evidence honestly and decides to act. The first resource any town must draw on is not water or fish or timber. It is the willingness of its people to question what no longer works.

readings.title: How Scientists Read a Coastline
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
How do you prove that a coastline is in trouble? You cannot simply say that the sea looks dirty or that there seem to be fewer fish than before. Feelings and impressions, however sincere, convince nobody who does not already agree with you. What persuades people is evidence: careful, precise measurements collected over time and presented honestly. Learning to gather and judge evidence is one of the most valuable skills you will ever develop, in science and far beyond it.
Environmental scientists usually begin with water. They collect samples at several points along the shore, because a single sample can mislead: water near the harbour may be filthy while water near the headland is clean. They measure the pH level, which shows how acidic the water has become, and they record the temperature, the clarity and the amount of dissolved oxygen. Then they repeat the same tests, at the same places, week after week. Repetition is what turns a number into a pattern, and patterns reveal whether conditions are improving or declining.
Counting fish requires different tactics. Researchers interview fishing crews about the size of their catches, examine market records going back years, and sometimes dive along measured lines to count what they see. No single method is perfect, so careful researchers combine several and compare the results. When independent methods point to the same conclusion, the conclusion becomes credible. When they disagree, an honest researcher says so and investigates further, rather than hiding the awkward number. Numbers also gain force when they are shown over time: a graph of five years of falling catches persuades far more powerfully than a single poor season, which sceptics could dismiss as unlucky weather.
Once the data is collected, the harder work begins: judging arguments. A claim is consistent when the evidence supports it and no statement contradicts another. It is inconsistent when the claim and the facts pull in opposite directions. Suppose an elder insists that the coastline is perfectly healthy, while the tests show dangerous pH levels and fish counts falling by half. Something is clearly amiss: the claim and the evidence cannot both be true. Or suppose someone declares that modern methods always bring dismal outcomes, while purification systems in neighbouring towns have plainly improved water quality. The word "always" makes a claim fragile, because one counter-example is enough to break it.
Careful thinkers also learn to discern the difference between an honest doubter and a closed mind. An honest doubter asks questions, examines the charts and changes position when the evidence demands it. A closed mind dismisses the findings without reading them, perhaps with a haughty wave of the hand or a terse remark. You cannot argue a closed mind open, but you can win over the honest doubters around it, and they are usually the majority.
Finally, evidence must be presented with respect, because data never speaks entirely for itself. The most effective presenters remain adamant about the facts while staying gentle with the people who doubt them. They attribute their conclusions to named sources, admit the limits of their data, and welcome questions instead of fearing them. In the end, copious charts and graphs matter less than trust. A community that trusts its young researchers will follow the numbers even when the numbers are uncomfortable, and that is how evidence, patiently gathered and honestly shared, becomes change.

readings.title: Shifting Currents, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The sea was still: pristine, at first glance. But Tariq knew better. A closer look revealed plastic bottles snagged in old fishing nets and sweet wrappers drifting near the ancient coral rocks.
The town of Marka rested along the shoreline like an old friend who had seen better days. Once a thriving hub of fishing and family gatherings on the sand, the coastline had become a quiet shadow of its former self. The transition from small-scale traditional fishing to larger commercial boats had changed the rhythm of life, and the waste along the beach had started to surpass what the sea could naturally break down.
Still, every morning at sunrise, Tariq jogged along the shore, noting what others missed. "They think it is clean," he muttered, pausing to pick up a straw. "But it is a deceptive beauty."
Back home, his sister Zara sat by the window with a cup of spiced tea, scribbling in a notebook. Her school was organising an environmental debate.
"Topic: traditional practice against modern policy," she read aloud. "We have to present both sides."
"Why both?" Tariq asked. "The old ways failed us."
"Some would disagree," she replied. "They think change is disrespectful."
Their grandfather entered the room, his walking stick tapping gently on the tiled floor. "You two speak as if nature is new. In my day, no one needed science to respect the sea. The antonym of respect is not science—it is carelessness."
"True," Tariq said gently. "But now we have evidence. Pollution. Fish loss."
Grandfather frowned. "The sea will heal, if left alone."
At school, Tariq joined the Green Guardians Club, a dedicated group of students researching the coastline's decline. He was surprised how quickly the group formed a bond, driven by a shared purpose.
Their leader, Amara, was adamant that they collect precise data. "We cannot just feel sad. We need to prove what is happening."
They tested water samples and documented fish populations. "This part smells awful," one student said, holding a tube up to the light.
"That is the pristine part—gone," Tariq replied.
Still, he often faltered when speaking to older residents. Many clung to the belief that their old ways were flawless.
"Your tactics are too aggressive," said one shopkeeper. "We have always thrown our waste behind the market. What is the harm?"
"It flows into the sea," Tariq explained. "And pretending otherwise will avail us nothing once the fish are gone."
Some nodded slowly. Others shook their heads. Tariq could sense something amiss in the way certain elders dismissed the findings without even glancing at the evidence.
One evening, the club reviewed all the coastal data, spread across a table in copious charts and graphs. The pH levels were dangerously off. Fish counts were down by nearly half. The figures spoke clearly, yet the town's mood remained sombre.
"I do not understand," said a member named Dina. "The evidence is right here. Why does no one believe us?"
"It is not just about facts," Amara replied. "Some people follow an older doctrine—one that says any change is disrespect. To them, we are just noisy children."
Over time, Tariq learned to discern the difference between genuine concern for tradition and stubborn refusal to accept evidence. Not everyone who disagreed was wrong; some simply needed more time and more patient conversation.
Amara suggested a formal presentation in the community hall near the harbour. "We show them everything," she said. "The charts, the samples, the counts. All of it."
"But will anyone come?" a student asked.
"If we do nothing," Amara replied, "our message will subside like the wind."

readings.title: Shifting Currents, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
They planned for weeks. Posters went up in every street, and flyers were handed out at the Friday market. Tariq rehearsed his speech with persistent effort. He memorised key phrases and practised pauses, adjusting his tone each time. He knew they needed to modify their approach: not abandon their message, but present it in a way that respected the elders while still delivering the truth.
"I should have practised public speaking more," he said nervously the night before the event.
"You are doing fine," Zara encouraged. "Just be yourself. Not too terse, but not long-winded either."
Finally, the day arrived. Chairs filled slowly inside the large community hall. A few elders sat with folded arms. Others leaned forward with interest. The town's mayor even arrived, bringing with her a small team of councillors.
Tariq stood at the front, his heart beating fast.
"This coastline is not dying. It is being killed. Not on purpose, perhaps, but by habit. Tradition is important, yes. But when habits hurt, they must be questioned."
He projected slides showing algae blooms and piles of dead fish washed up on the sand. "This is the egregious result of ignorance, not evil. And we have the power to change it."
A murmur ran through the crowd. One man stood up. "You blame us. But what have you done?"
Amara stepped up beside Tariq. "We test. We clean. We educate. And we ask you to help us pivot—to change not our values, but our methods."
She pointed to a small boy in the front row. "He helped gather water samples. He skipped cartoons for this."
Laughter rippled through the room, lightening the mood.
Over the weeks that followed, something shifted. Younger children helped collect waste along the beach. Some shopkeepers placed bins outside their stores. A local tailor even designed reusable bags printed with coastal slogans in two languages.
But resistance remained. One haughty elder looked at the students with open disdain and refused to attend any further meetings. A community leader who misunderstood the movement claimed it mocked the elders. "It insults our doctrine of stewardship," he argued at the evening gathering. "Modern ways bring dismal outcomes."
"They should have joined us," Amara said, her eyes flashing. "Instead they speak in anger."
"They are not bad people," Tariq said quietly. "Just naive about the science."
Still, not everyone could be reached. One afternoon, an old man shouted at Tariq as he was picking up rubbish near the harbour. "Go lecture somewhere else!"
Tariq walked away, his heart heavy. "Maybe it has all gone awry," he whispered.
Zara disagreed. "Look again." She pointed across the beach to a small boy carefully picking up plastic wrappers and placing them in a bag. "You have instilled new habits in people. That matters more than you realise."
A month later, Tariq was invited to speak at the regional youth summit in the capital. He wore a clean white shirt and shoes that felt a little threadbare, but he stood tall at the podium.
"We believed the sea was healthy because it looked blue," he said to the packed hall. "But beneath the surface, we found decay. Some data had been hidden. Some opinions were loud but not credible."
He paused and looked out at the audience. "Although many resisted change, we remained adamant. Not out of pride, but out of hope."
His speech earned a standing ovation. Later, a local radio host asked him, "What do you attribute your success to?"
Tariq thought for a moment. "To listening. To questioning. And to never letting doubt make our progress falter."
In the following months, grants were secured for the town. Solar-powered water purification systems were ordered from the capital. According to the mayor, "The first units will be installed by December." Amara reported that the council had confirmed the timeline, and she stated that the transition to cleaner water management had already begun.

readings.title: Shifting Currents, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Amara was invited to join the national youth council for environmental leadership. Tariq received an internship at a marine research centre near the coast.
At home, Tariq's grandfather started walking with him along the shore again, just as they had done when Tariq was a small child. For a long while they walked in silence, watching the tide fold and unfold along the sand.
"You were right," the old man said softly. "Change does not mean disrespect. It means survival."
Tariq nodded. "We should have listened to each other sooner."
On a quiet Thursday morning, Tariq visited the shore alone. A heron lifted its wings and glided low over the surface of the water. The air was still, but not dead. It was alive with momentum, slow but sure.
He thought about dialects, and about how people can say the same thing in different words. Maybe the word "clean" meant something different to his grandfather. Maybe "progress" felt like loss to some elders. Perhaps every generation speaks its own dialect of care, and the real work is learning to translate.
But in every tongue, care was still care. And in every heart, the sea had meaning.
Tariq smiled and whispered a quiet word of thanks. The currents were shifting—not just in the water, but in the minds and hearts of his community.

grammar.title: What Is a Complex Noun Phrase?
grammar.explanation: A complex noun phrase is a group of words built around a head noun, and the extra words give detailed information about a person, place, thing or idea. Writers use complex noun phrases to pack meaning into fewer words, which makes academic writing more efficient and more sophisticated.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A complex noun phrase is a head noun plus its modifiers.
Simple: The mistake caused damage.
Complex: The egregious environmental mistake that went unnoticed for years caused damage.
The second sentence tells us far more about the mistake: it was egregious, it was environmental, and it went unnoticed for years.
Modifiers placed before the noun are called pre-modifiers: the pristine blue water.
Modifiers placed after the noun are called post-modifiers: the water in the lake, the boy who helped gather samples.
Why it matters: instead of three short sentences (There was a mistake. It was environmental. It was serious.), one strong sentence carries everything: The serious environmental mistake caused widespread damage.
grammar.commonMistake: A complex noun phrase is still not a sentence on its own. 'The egregious environmental mistake that went unnoticed for years' names something but says nothing about it, so it always needs a main verb: the mistake caused damage.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a target: the head noun sits at the centre, and every modifier is a ring around it. However many rings you add, the arrow must still hit the noun.
grammar.practice:
Part A - copy each sentence and underline the complex noun phrase, then circle the head noun: 1) The persistent young student from Marka won the debate. 2) They tested a pristine water sample collected near the rocks. 3) The copious charts spread across the old wooden table showed alarming results. 4) A haughty shopkeeper who refused to listen walked away. 5) The solar-powered purification systems ordered from the capital will arrive soon.
Part B - write two sentences of your own about this unit's story, each containing a complex noun phrase with at least two modifiers.

Answer Key (self-check):
Part A - complex noun phrase, with the head noun in CAPS: 1) The persistent young STUDENT from Marka. 2) a pristine water SAMPLE collected near the rocks. 3) The copious CHARTS spread across the old wooden table. 4) A haughty SHOPKEEPER who refused to listen. 5) The solar-powered purification SYSTEMS ordered from the capital.
Part B is open-ended (your own sentences), so there is no single correct answer. Self-check with a model: 'The exhausted, determined students collected samples from the shrinking bay.' Ask yourself: can I point to one head noun, and are there at least two modifiers built around it (before it, after it, or both)?

grammar.title: Building Complex Noun Phrases
grammar.explanation: You build a complex noun phrase in layers: start with the head noun, add a determiner, add adjectives in front, then attach phrases or clauses behind. Each layer sharpens the picture without starting a new sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Layer 1, the head noun: water, mistake, data, boy.
Layer 2, a determiner: the water, a mistake.
Layer 3, pre-modifiers (adjectives): the pristine water, the egregious environmental mistake.
Layer 4, post-modifiers: the pristine water in the lake; the boy who helped gather samples; the waste thrown behind the market; the students researching the decline.
Order of adjectives before a noun: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Say a beautiful large old Somali fishing boat, never a fishing old large beautiful Somali boat.
Post-modifier types: prepositional phrase (the town along the coastline), relative clause (the evidence that proved the pollution), past participle phrase (the systems ordered from the capital), present participle phrase (the wind blowing across the shore).
From the story: 'a dedicated group of students researching the coastline's decline' has the head noun group, the pre-modifier dedicated, and the post-modifiers of students and researching the coastline's decline; 'the egregious result of ignorance' has the head noun result; 'a small team of councillors' has the head noun team.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often reverse the adjective order and write 'an environmental egregious mistake'; opinion adjectives such as egregious come before category adjectives such as environmental, so the natural order is 'an egregious environmental mistake'.
grammar.memoryTip: Opinion first, category last: how you FEEL about it comes before WHAT KIND it is, as in an egregious (feeling) environmental (kind) mistake.
grammar.practice:
Part A - expand each bare noun into a complex noun phrase with at least two modifiers: 1) the mistake, 2) a student, 3) the water, 4) the presentation, 5) a bag.
Part B - rebuild each jumbled phrase in the natural adjective order: 6) boat / fishing / small / the; 7) bags / cotton / reusable / two; 8) table / wooden / old / the.
Part C - add one post-modifier of the stated type: 9) the charts (add a prepositional phrase); 10) the boy (add a relative clause); 11) the systems (add a past participle phrase).

Answer Key (self-check):
Part A is open-ended composition, so mark yourself against the four-layer method above (head noun, determiner, pre-modifiers, post-modifiers) rather than a fixed answer. Model expansions: 1) the mistake -> 'the egregious environmental mistake'; 2) a student -> 'a persistent young student researching the coastline'; 3) the water -> 'the pristine blue water near the reef'; 4) the presentation -> 'the sombre, data-heavy presentation on pollution'; 5) a bag -> 'a reusable cotton bag from the market'.
Part B (fixed adjective order - opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose): 6) the small fishing boat. 7) two reusable cotton bags. 8) the old wooden table.
Part C is open-ended; match the post-modifier type named in each item. Models: 9) prepositional phrase - 'the charts on the classroom wall'; 10) relative clause - 'the boy who collected the samples'; 11) past participle phrase - 'the systems installed last December'.

grammar.title: Noun Phrase Pitfalls
grammar.explanation: Four pitfalls cause most noun-phrase errors: wrong adjective order, missing determiners, overloaded phrases, and the wrong relative pronoun. All four are easy to fix once you can spot them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Pitfall 1, wrong adjective order: say 'an egregious environmental mistake', because opinion comes before category.
Pitfall 2, missing determiner: 'I found pristine water in lake' needs one, so write 'I found pristine water in the lake.'
Pitfall 3, overloading: 'the very extremely incredibly large old broken dark wooden fishing boat' buries the noun; two or three modifiers are usually enough.
Pitfall 4, the wrong relative pronoun: who is for people, which is for things, and that can serve for either, so 'the boy which helped' must become 'the boy who helped'.
grammar.commonMistake: The overload trap is the sneakiest: adding a fourth and fifth adjective feels impressive but makes the phrase harder to read, and examiners reward control, not decoration.
grammar.memoryTip: Fix the order, add the determiner, cut to three modifiers, match who to people: four quick checks, one clean phrase.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each sentence so the noun phrase is correct: 1) The boy which helped gather samples was praised. 2) She bought a dusty old from the market book. 3) The fishing small boat sailed across the bay. 4) We found pristine water in lake near the farm. 5) An group adamant of students protested the decision. 6) The very extremely incredibly heavy old broken dark wooden fishing boat finally sank.
Then write one sentence describing the harbour using exactly three well-ordered modifiers.

Answer Key (self-check):
1) The boy who helped gather samples was praised. 2) She bought a dusty old book from the market. 3) The small fishing boat sailed across the bay. 4) We found pristine water in the lake near the farm. 5) An adamant group of students protested the decision. 6) Overload trimmed to two or three modifiers, for example: 'The heavy, old fishing boat finally sank.' (Any version keeping only two or three well-chosen modifiers, in the correct order, is correct - the point is cutting the pile-up, not matching exact words.)
The closing task (one sentence about the harbour with exactly three well-ordered modifiers) is open-ended. Model: 'The busy, old, Somali harbour buzzed with fishermen' (opinion, age, origin). Self-check: exactly three modifiers, in opinion/size/age/shape/colour/origin/material/purpose order.

grammar.title: The Future Passive
grammar.explanation: The future passive describes what will happen when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown or obvious. It appears constantly in formal plans, news reports and official announcements.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + will be + past participle, with 'by + doer' only when the doer matters.
Active: The council will install the purification systems. (focus on the council)
Passive: The purification systems will be installed by the council. (focus on the systems)
How to transform: take the object of the active sentence, make it the subject, add will be, then the past participle, then 'by + doer' if needed.
Active: Scientists will test the water samples. Passive: The water samples will be tested (by scientists).
From the story: 'The first units will be installed by December.' Compare the past passives nearby: 'Grants were secured for the town' and 'Solar-powered water purification systems were ordered from the capital.'
grammar.commonMistake: The classic slip is dropping 'be': 'The homework will finished' must be 'The homework will be finished', and the verb must be a past participle, so write 'the project will be completed', not 'will be complete'.
grammar.memoryTip: WILL BE DONE: three words, three checks. Will points to the future, be must never be skipped, done must be a past participle.
grammar.practice:
Part A - complete each sentence in the future passive: 1) The new bins ______ (deliver) to the market next week. 2) A report on water quality ______ (publish) by the research team. 3) The community hall ______ (clean) before the presentation. 4) Reusable bags ______ (distribute) to every household. 5) The damaged fishing nets ______ (replace) by the end of the month.
Part B - rewrite in the future passive: 6) The mayor will open the new recycling centre. 7) Students will present the findings at the summit. 8) The government will fund the clean-up programme. 9) Engineers will build a new water treatment plant. 10) Volunteers will collect plastic waste from the beach.

Answer Key (self-check):
Part A: 1) will be delivered. 2) will be published. 3) will be cleaned. 4) will be distributed. 5) will be replaced.
Part B: 6) The new recycling centre will be opened by the mayor. 7) The findings will be presented at the summit by students. 8) The clean-up programme will be funded by the government. 9) A new water treatment plant will be built by engineers. 10) Plastic waste will be collected from the beach by volunteers. (Dropping 'by + doer' is also acceptable when the doer is already obvious, as the rule above explains.)

grammar.title: Connectives for Contrast and Purpose
grammar.explanation: Connectives are the words that join ideas and show the relationship between them: contrast connectives signal that the second idea is different or surprising, while purpose connectives explain why an action is done.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Contrast connectives: although / though / even though (Although it was raining, we continued the clean-up.); however (The data was clear. However, many people still disagreed.); yet (The evidence was strong, yet the town's mood remained sombre.); despite / in spite of (Despite the resistance, the students kept working.); while / whereas (While Tariq believed in science, his grandfather trusted tradition.); on the other hand (Some supported the project. On the other hand, others were sceptical.)
Purpose connectives: in order to (They collected data in order to prove the pollution was real.); so that (She practised every day so that she could speak confidently.); to (He jogged the shore to note what others missed.); so as to (They modified their approach so as to gain the elders' trust.)
Key rule: although already signals contrast, so never add but. Write 'Although it was cold, we went outside', with no but.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers double up with 'Although it was cold, but we went outside'; the two contrast signals fight each other, so keep although and delete but.
grammar.memoryTip: Contrast turns the argument and purpose explains the action: BUT-words bend the sentence, TO-words tell you why.
grammar.practice:
Part A - fill each blank with the best connective from: although, however, in order to, so that, yet, despite. 1) ______ the evidence was clear, many people refused to change. 2) Tariq rehearsed his speech ______ he could deliver it confidently. 3) The students worked hard. ______, not everyone listened. 4) They placed bins outside ______ reduce waste. 5) ______ the resistance from elders, the club continued their work. 6) The figures spoke clearly, ______ the mood remained sombre.
Part B - join each pair with the connective in brackets: 7) The sea looked blue and clean. It was actually polluted. (although) 8) Amara studied the data carefully. She wanted to find the truth. (in order to) 9) Tariq was nervous. He gave an excellent speech. (despite) 10) The students made posters. They wanted everyone to attend. (so that)

Answer Key (self-check):
Part A: 1) Although. 2) so that. 3) However. 4) in order to. 5) Despite. 6) yet.
Part B: 7) Although the sea looked blue and clean, it was actually polluted. 8) Amara studied the data carefully in order to find the truth. 9) Despite feeling nervous, Tariq gave an excellent speech. (Since 'despite' takes a noun or -ing form, not a full clause, 'Despite his nerves' or 'Despite feeling nervous' are both correct - not 'Despite he was nervous'.) 10) The students made posters so that everyone would attend.

grammar.title: Past Modals, Reported Speech and Spotting Inconsistencies
grammar.explanation: This lesson gathers three tools for thinking about the past and about other people's words: should have for regret and advice, reported speech for retelling what was said, and consistency checks for judging whether an argument holds together.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Past modals: should have + past participle means it was the right thing, but it did not happen ('I should have practised public speaking more'); should not have + past participle means it happened, but it was wrong ('They should not have thrown waste into the sea'). Do not confuse should have (regret) with must have (deduction: 'She must have left early').
Reported speech: shift the tense back, change the pronouns and adjust time expressions. 'I am happy' becomes she said she was happy; 'I will help' becomes he said he would help; 'I can swim' becomes she said she could swim. From the story: the mayor said that the first units would be installed by December, and Amara stated that the transition had already begun.
Spotting inconsistencies: identify the claim, check the evidence, look for contradictions, then judge. If an elder claims the coastline is perfectly healthy while the tests show dangerous pH levels and falling fish counts, the claim and the evidence cannot both be true. Absolute words such as always and never make claims fragile, because one counter-example breaks them.
grammar.commonMistake: In past modals the 'have' often vanishes ('they should practised') or the participle slips back to the base form ('she should have tell me'); the full pattern is always should + have + past participle, as in they should have practised and she should have told me.
grammar.memoryTip: SHOULD HAVE looks backwards with regret, SAID plus a past tense passes words along, and CLAIM versus EVIDENCE decides who to believe.
grammar.practice:
Part A - complete with should have or should not have and the correct participle: 1) We ______ (start) the clean-up earlier. 2) They ______ (throw) their rubbish into the sea. 3) Tariq ______ (prepare) his notes the night before. 4) The council ______ (ignore) the students' report. 5) She ______ (bring) more water samples to the meeting.
Part B - convert to reported speech: 6) Tariq said, 'I will speak at the summit.' 7) Amara said, 'We need precise data.' 8) Zara asked, 'Are you nervous?' 9) Grandfather said, 'The sea will heal.' 10) The shopkeeper asked, 'What have you done?'
Part C - explain the inconsistency in each pair: 11) Claim: 'Our coastline is perfectly healthy.' Evidence: water tests show dangerous pH levels and declining fish populations. 12) Claim: 'Young people have done nothing to help.' Evidence: students have tested water, cleaned the beach and educated the community for months. 13) Claim: 'Modern methods always bring dismal outcomes.' Evidence: purification systems have improved water quality in many other towns.

Answer Key (self-check):
Part A: 1) should have started. 2) should not have thrown. 3) should have prepared. 4) should not have ignored. 5) should have brought.
Part B (reported speech - tense shifts back, pronouns change to fit the reporter): 6) Tariq said (that) he would speak at the summit. 7) Amara said (that) they needed precise data. 8) Zara asked if/whether he or she was nervous. 9) Grandfather said (that) the sea would heal. 10) The shopkeeper asked what he or she had done.
Part C is open-ended explanation, so check that your answer names the contradiction and, where relevant, the absolute word it breaks: 11) 'Perfectly healthy' cannot be true alongside dangerous pH levels and falling fish counts - the evidence directly contradicts the claim. 12) 'Have done nothing' is broken by the evidence that students tested water, cleaned the beach and educated the community for months. 13) 'Always bring dismal outcomes' is an absolute claim that one counter-example disproves - purification systems have already improved water quality in other towns.

1) Do you agree with Tariq that traditional practices should be questioned when they cause harm? Explain your reasoning.

3) Amara says, 'If we do nothing, our message will subside like the wind.' Describe a time when you stayed silent about something important. What happened?

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Persuasive Mini-Speech
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Prepare a persuasive speech of one to two minutes on one of these topics: 1) Why our school should start a recycling programme. 2) What our community should have done differently to protect local water sources. 3) Although technology can help the environment, people must also change their habits. 4) The most important natural resource in our region and why it must be protected.
Your speech must include one complex noun phrase, one future passive sentence, one connective for contrast or purpose, and one past modal.
Structure: an opening that states your argument in one or two sentences; a body with two or three supported points; a conclusion with a call to action or a thought-provoking question.
Practise at least three times, time yourself, and record yourself or ask a family member to listen.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Role Play
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Role-play one of these scenarios with a partner or with your AI tutor:
1) Tariq and the shopkeeper: Tariq persuades a shopkeeper to stop throwing waste behind the market, while the shopkeeper defends the old ways. Use connectives for contrast: although, however, yet.
2) Amara and a sceptical elder: Amara explains the scientific evidence to an elder who trusts traditional stewardship. Use complex noun phrases to describe the evidence, such as 'the precise data collected from multiple water samples'.
3) Tariq and a radio host: the host interviews Tariq about the campaign, and Tariq reflects on what the community should have done earlier. Use past modals in your answers.
Afterwards, reflect: did you use the target grammar, and did you sound natural?
Pronunciation focus. Stress the capitalised syllable: pristine (pris-TEEN), egregious (eh-GREE-jus), adamant (AD-uh-munt), doctrine (DOK-trin), deceptive (deh-SEP-tiv), copious (KOH-pee-us), threadbare (THRED-bair), discern (dih-SURN).

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Debate Performance

writing.title: Writing 1: Descriptive Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a descriptive paragraph of 100-150 words about a natural place you have visited or know well: a beach, a river, a forest, a garden, or any outdoor space. Use at least three complex noun phrases and five vocabulary words from this unit.
Plan first: choose the place; list sensory details (what you see, hear, smell and feel there); choose vocabulary that fits naturally, so the place might be pristine, or something there may have gone awry; build complex noun phrases ('the tall, ancient trees along the riverbank', not just 'the trees').
Open with a topic sentence that introduces the place, support it with descriptive sentences, and close with a sentence that expresses your feelings about it.
Example opening: 'The wide, sandy beach near my grandmother's house is one of the most pristine places I have ever seen.'

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: pristine opens the story ('The sea was still: pristine, at first glance') and returns in the sample scene ('That is the pristine part—gone'); faltered describes Tariq's nerves with older residents; adamant is Amara insisting on precise data; copious describes the charts and graphs on the club's table; egregious is Tariq's town-hall phrase 'the egregious result of ignorance'; threadbare describes his shoes at the summit; instilled is Zara's line 'You have instilled new habits in people'; credible appears in 'Some opinions were loud but not credible'; doctrine covers the elders' 'older doctrine' and 'doctrine of stewardship'; discern closes part 1 as Tariq learns to discern concern from refusal. Accept any new learner sentence that uses the word accurately in a fresh context.

Model answers from the story. Complex noun phrase: 'a dedicated group of students researching the coastline's decline'. Future passive: 'The first units will be installed by December.' Contrast connective: 'Although many resisted change, we remained adamant.' Past modal: 'I should have practised public speaking more' or 'They should have joined us.' Reported speech conversion: direct 'The sea will heal, if left alone' becomes Grandfather said that the sea would heal if it was left alone. Accept any accurate example plus a correctly shifted conversion.

Strong FOR arguments: the evidence shows real harm (falling fish counts, dangerous pH); stewardship itself demands adaptation; communities that modified their methods recovered. Strong AGAINST arguments: tradition carries tested wisdom; rapid change can damage trust and identity; evidence can be incomplete, so caution is reasonable. Award credit when each argument carries a support sentence using a unit grammar pattern, and require at least one although or despite acknowledgement of the other side.

Sample expansions: 1) The persistent young students from the Green Guardians Club presented their findings. 2) We tested the murky brown water collected near the harbour. 3) The haughty old man who refused to look at the evidence disagreed with Tariq. 4) Amara designed an ambitious community recycling programme for the entire coastline. 5) The small coastal town battered by years of pollution needs help. Accept any grammatical phrase with at least two modifiers around the head noun.

1) The beach will be cleaned by the volunteers. 2) The project will be funded by the government. 3) The data will be presented at the conference (by students). 4) Solar panels will be installed on the school roof (by engineers). 5) A new environmental committee will be elected by the community. The 'by' phrase may be dropped wherever the doer is obvious.
1) in order to, 2) so that, 3) Although, 4) Despite, 5) yet, 6) However. Items 3, 4 and 6 open their sentences and need capital letters; 'yet' follows a comma inside its sentence.
Correct answer: to hesitate or lose strength when doing something. Tariq faltered when speaking to older residents, and at the summit he vows never to let doubt make their progress falter.
Correct answer: clean, fresh, and in its original condition; not spoiled or damaged. The sea only looked pristine; up close the litter showed.
Correct answer: making someone believe something that is not true; misleading. The calm blue surface was a deceptive beauty hiding decay.
Correct answer: lacking experience or sophistication; easily fooled or deceived. Tariq calls the resisters naive about the science, not bad people.
Correct answer: persistent. Rehearsing key phrases and pauses again and again is effort that continues despite difficulty.
Correct answer: antonym. Grandfather names the true opposite of respect: carelessness, not science.
Correct answer: deceptive. Tariq means the beauty misleads people into thinking the sea is clean.
Correct answer: egregious. Tariq names a shockingly bad outcome of ignorance rather than deliberate evil.
